controlLoop.title: From measurement to feedback control.
controlLoop.subtitle: An interactive view of the control concepts behind instrumentation, automation and PID systems.

panel1.title: High-Level Control Cycle
panel1.caption: Sensor → Controller → Actuator → Process → Feedback
panel1.infoSensor: Measures the process variable (PV) and converts it to a usable signal.
panel1.infoController: Compares SP with PV, computes error, outputs control action.
panel1.infoActuator: Final control element (valve, motor, heater) applies output to process.
panel1.infoProcess: The physical process being controlled (tank, reactor, etc.)

panel2.title: Closed-Loop PID System
panel2.caption: SP → Σ → PID → Actuator → Process → Sensor → PV → Σ (feedback)
panel2.infoPID: Computes control output: P·e + I∫e + D·de/dt where e = SP - PV.
panel2.explainIntro: The controller recalculates its output every cycle from five numbers. Here's the same math the diagram above is running, broken into steps, with the live values plugged in.
panel2.explainStep1Title: Error — how far off the setpoint is
panel2.explainStep2Title: Proportional (P) — reacts to the error right now
panel2.explainStep5Title: Output — what actually drives the heater
panel2.spHint: Try it — change the target temperature and watch the loop respond
panel2.exampleTitle: Example: temperature control of a heated chamber
panel2.exampleDesc: An electric heater warms a chamber toward a target temperature (the set point). A temperature sensor reports the actual value, and the PID controller adjusts the heater power to close the gap. The same loop is used in poultry brooders and incubators, industrial ovens and kilns, and the heating zones of plastic extruders. Here it is a simulation with a simple thermal model — the chamber starts at room temperature (20 °C) and the heater, at full power, can reach about 65 °C.
panel2.spLimitMax: Limited to 65 °C — the heater can't heat the chamber any higher.
panel2.spLimitMin: Limited to 20 °C — a heater can't cool below room temperature.

coopmaster.title: CoopMaster — Smart Connected Poultry Coop
coopmaster.desc: A Raspberry Pi-based automation system combining sensors, actuators, camera monitoring and a Flutter companion app.

detail.overview: CoopMaster is a smart connected poultry-coop automation and monitoring system developed as an engineering graduation project. The objective was to design a low-cost, practical, and reliable solution capable of monitoring important environmental conditions inside a poultry coop while automating several repetitive tasks that normally require manual intervention. The project combines embedded systems, industrial-style automation, sensors, actuators, networking, cloud services, mobile application development, and local safety mechanisms into one integrated system. Rather than treating the poultry coop as a simple IoT demonstration, CoopMaster was designed around an engineering principle: the system should remain useful and safe even when the network or cloud service is unavailable. The system uses a Raspberry Pi 5 as the main local controller, Python for hardware and automation logic, sensors for monitoring, relays and actuators for physical control, Firebase for cloud synchronization, and a Flutter application for remote monitoring.

problem.title: The Problem
problem.intro: Traditional small poultry coops often require the owner to manually perform several repetitive tasks. Depending on the installation, the owner may need to:
tasks: Check whether the coop door is open or closed
Open or close the entrance manually
Check whether rain is occurring before opening an external entrance
Monitor the general operating state of the installation
Visit the coop physically to verify that equipment is operating correctly
problem.challenge: The main challenge was designing a system in which: Sensors provide information → the controller interprets that information → automation logic makes decisions → actuators execute the required actions → the system reports its state to the user. This creates a complete closed-loop automation architecture.

objectives.title: Main Objectives
items: Environmental and state monitoring — collect information from sensors and determine the current state
Automatic door management — open and close the entrance automatically according to predefined conditions
Rain-aware operation — detect rain conditions and use this information to avoid inappropriate door operation
Motion detection — use a PIR sensor to detect movement in the monitored area
Watering control — control a water pump to activate watering-related equipment without direct manual operation
Remote monitoring — monitor through a graphical mobile interface
Local operation — retain essential functionality when Internet connectivity is unavailable
Safety — avoid blindly commanding actuators without verifying the state of the installation
Low-cost implementation — use accessible and relatively inexpensive components while applying engineering principles

architecture.title: System Architecture
architecture.intro: CoopMaster is organized into several interconnected layers.

physical.title: 1. Physical Layer
physical.desc: Contains the real-world sensors and actuators. Sensors transform physical events into electrical signals that can be interpreted by the controller.

control.title: 2. Control Layer
control.desc: The Raspberry Pi 5 acts as the main local controller. It reads sensor inputs, processes sensor states, executes automation rules, controls actuators, monitors equipment states, handles local safety logic, communicates with the cloud layer, and provides information to the user interface.
responsibilities: Providing information to the user interface

software.title: 3. Software Layer
software.desc: The local control software was developed using Python. The raw GPIO states are converted into meaningful logical information.

actuator.title: 4. Actuator Layer
actuator.desc: The controller communicates with physical actuators through appropriate switching interfaces. Relay interfaces separate low-power control signals from higher-power actuator circuits.

gpio.title: GPIO Configuration
gpio.intro: An important aspect of the prototype was defining a clear mapping between the Raspberry Pi GPIO pins and the physical devices.

table.note: The exact electrical implementation is separated from the software logic through the GPIO abstraction, making it easier to change hardware later.

doorAutomation.title: Door Automation
doorAutomation.intro: One of the main functions of CoopMaster is automated door control. The door system is not treated as a simple OPEN = motor ON logic.
doorAutomation.note: This feedback-based architecture is important because an automation controller should ideally know whether the commanded action actually occurred.

safety.title: Door Safety Logic
safety.intro: Safety was one of the most important design considerations. A naive implementation could simply activate a motor for a fixed amount of time, but this creates several problems.
safety.approach: Instead of relying only on time, the system uses sensor information to determine whether the door has reached its intended state. This represents an important transition from simple remote control toward feedback-based automation.

rainDetection.title: Rain Detection
rainDetection.intro: The rain sensor provides information about the external environmental condition. The controller can use this information as part of the automation decision. Conceptually: Rain sensor → Raspberry Pi → Automation logic → Door decision.

motionDetection.title: Motion Detection
motionDetection.intro: A PIR sensor is used to detect movement. The sensor is connected to GPIO 5. The PIR signal allows the controller to determine whether motion has been detected in the monitored area.

pumpControl.title: Water Pump Control
pumpControl.intro: CoopMaster also includes control of a watering system. The water-related control path uses: Controller → switching interface → pump. The pump can therefore be activated by software rather than requiring direct manual switching.

localFirst.title: Local-First Architecture
localFirst.intro: One of the strongest engineering concepts in CoopMaster is its local-first architecture. Many IoT projects depend heavily on cloud services. If the Internet connection disappears, critical automation may stop functioning.
localFirst.cloudDependent: Sensor → Internet → Cloud → Application → Internet → Controller → Actuator
localFirst.coopmasterLocal: Sensor → Raspberry Pi → Local automation → Actuator

firebase.title: Firebase Integration
firebase.intro: Firebase is used as the cloud connectivity layer. The Raspberry Pi communicates relevant system information to the cloud, while the Flutter application can use that information to provide the user with a remote view of the installation.

flutter.title: Flutter Mobile Application
flutter.intro: A dedicated application was developed using Flutter. The application provides a graphical interface for interacting with the CoopMaster system. Instead of requiring the user to understand GPIO states, relay states, or Python processes, the application translates the technical information into a more understandable interface.
features: System status — a quick overview of the current installation state
Door control — the user can request opening or closing

comms.title: Hardware-to-Software Communication
comms.intro: One of the most important aspects of CoopMaster is the complete communication chain between the physical world and the software. For example, consider the rain sensor:
chain: Sensor — The rain sensor changes its electrical state
Raspberry Pi — The GPIO input detects the change
Python — The Python control program interprets the signal
Automation logic — The system determines what action should be taken
Actuator — The relevant relay/motor state is controlled
Firebase — The updated state can be synchronized
Flutter — The user can see the updated condition in the application

engineering.title: Engineering Control Philosophy
engineering.intro: Although CoopMaster is a small-scale project, its architecture follows principles found in industrial automation. The fundamental chain is: SENSOR → CONTROLLER → ACTUATOR.
engineering.understanding: The project demonstrates an understanding that automation is not simply about writing code or switching a motor. It requires understanding the relationship between physical processes, sensors, electrical signals, controllers, actuators, feedback, communication, safety, and user interfaces.

instrumentation.title: Instrumentation Perspective
instrumentation.intro: From an instrumentation perspective, CoopMaster can be viewed as a small process-control installation. The physical environment represents the process. Sensors provide measurements or states. The Raspberry Pi acts as the control unit. Relays and motors provide the actuation layer. The Flutter application acts as the supervisory/user interface. Firebase provides the communication and remote data layer.
instrumentation.architecture: PROCESS → SENSORS → SIGNAL ACQUISITION → CONTROLLER → CONTROL LOGIC → ACTUATORS → PROCESS, with an additional monitoring path: CONTROLLER → CLOUD → USER APPLICATION.

safetyPhilosophy.title: Safety Philosophy
safetyPhilosophy.intro: Safety was considered at both the software and system levels. The system should not assume that a command was successfully executed simply because a command was sent.
safetyPhilosophy.distinction: Command: CLOSE DOOR does not automatically mean Door = CLOSED. The system should use feedback to determine the actual state. This distinction between commanded state and actual state is an important engineering concept.

fault.title: Fault and Connectivity Considerations
fault.intro: A major consideration in the architecture was the possibility of communication failure. Internet connectivity can be interrupted for many reasons. Therefore, critical local functions should not depend on constant cloud availability.
fault.cloudFailure: Remote monitoring may be temporarily unavailable, but the local automation can continue.
fault.localFailure: This is more serious because the controller is responsible for physical automation.

raspberryPi.title: Why Raspberry Pi?
raspberryPi.intro: The Raspberry Pi 5 was selected as the main controller because it provides a useful balance between processing capability, GPIO access, Linux environment, Python compatibility, networking, development flexibility, low cost, and availability.
raspberryPi.distinction: A Raspberry Pi is not automatically equivalent to an industrial PLC. A PLC is designed specifically for industrial environments, deterministic control, electrical robustness, maintenance, and industrial communication.

development.title: Development Process
development.intro: The project was approached as an integrated engineering system rather than as isolated software and hardware tasks.

steps.desc: The first stage involved identifying repetitive manual operations that could benefit from automation.
The hardware and software components were organized into separate layers.
The sensors and actuators were connected to the Raspberry Pi GPIO system.
Python was used to implement the local automation logic.
The automation rules were implemented so that sensor information could influence actuator behavior.
Firebase was integrated to synchronize system information and enable remote access.
A user interface was created to make the system understandable to a non-technical user.
The system was tested by observing the interaction between all components.

challenges.title: Challenges

items.title: Actuator control

items.title: Feedback

items.title: Multiple technologies
items.desc: CoopMaster combines several technologies: Python + Raspberry Pi + GPIO + Firebase + Flutter.

future.title: Future Improvements
future.intro: Although the prototype successfully demonstrates the core concept, several improvements could make the system more robust.

items.title: Industrial controller migration
items.desc: The Raspberry Pi could eventually be replaced or complemented by an industrial PLC.

items.title: ESP32-C3 version

items.title: Improved industrial communication

items.title: More sensors

items.title: Historical data

items.title: Alarm management

items.title: Predictive maintenance
items.desc: With enough historical data, the system could identify abnormal equipment behavior.

finalSummary.title: Final Project Summary
finalSummary.text: CoopMaster is a connected smart poultry-coop automation system designed to demonstrate how embedded electronics, instrumentation, automation, cloud technologies, and software development can be combined to solve a practical real-world problem. The most important architectural decision is the use of a local-first control philosophy.

ats.eyebrow: Classic Electrical Control · Power Transfer · CADe SIMU
ats.title: ATS 3-Line Control Circuit
ats.cardDesc: A three-line transfer-control concept: utility, generator and test lines selected by three contactors with timers and interlocking, simulated in CADe SIMU.
ats.overview: This CADe SIMU project demonstrates a three-line transfer-control concept. The three-phase utility line has first priority, the generator line is the second choice, and the third line is a simulated test source used only for demonstration—not a real supply.
ats.principles: In the intended priority order, the controller selects the three-phase C line first. If it is unavailable, the generator line can be selected subject to R1/R2 logic and the 5-second delay. The H line is a simulated test option and should not override the utility or generator priority.
ats.loadnote: KM1, KM2 or KM3 connects the selected line to the load indicator, with interlocking intended to prevent multiple contactors from closing together.
ats.r1a: R1 monitors/controls the three-phase C line.
ats.r1b: Timer T1 is set to 5 seconds before commanding KM1.
ats.r1c: KM1 is interlocked with KM2 and KM3.
ats.r1d: The C line has priority over the other lines.
ats.r2a: R2 controls the generator G line.
ats.r2b: Timer T2 is set to 5 seconds before commanding KM2.
ats.r2c: KM2 is interlocked with KM1 and KM3.
ats.r2d: R1 priority logic prevents the generator line from taking priority over the available C line.
ats.km3a: The H line has no dedicated control relay in this simulation; its contactor coil is controlled directly by the designed control logic.
ats.km3b: KM3 is interlocked with the R1/R2 control logic and contactors KM1/KM2.
ats.km3c: This line is for testing only, not a real third power source.
ats.ledload: A separate LED connected to the contactor outputs represents the load.
ats.cmcb: control MCB for the three-phase C line
ats.gmcb: control MCB for the generator line
ats.hmcb: control MCB for the test line
ats.mccb: three-phase C-line power circuit, feeding KM1
ats.contactors: contactors for C, G and H lines respectively
ats.videoNote: Short, silent visual demonstration of the electrical schematic.
ats.c3: Electrical and, where required, mechanical interlocking
ats.c6: Cable sizing, short-circuit withstand, and protection coordination
ats.note: This is an educational CADe SIMU simulation. The H line and its MCB are test-only elements. The described 5-second timers and priority logic reflect the simulation as explained, not a certified ATS design. A real transfer system needs verified electrical interlocking, appropriate switching/protection ratings, source compatibility checks, and review against applicable standards before implementation.

fwdrev.eyebrow: Motor Control · Reversing · Star-Delta Starting · CADe SIMU
fwdrev.title: Forward/Reverse Star-Delta Starter
fwdrev.cardDesc: Power and control schematic of a forward/reverse star-delta starter for a three-phase induction motor, with a star-delta timer, overload protection and contactor interlocking.
fwdrev.overview: This project presents the power and control schematic for a forward/reverse star-delta starter for a three-phase induction motor, designed in CADe SIMU. The circuit uses forward/reverse contactors, a star-delta timer, push buttons, overload protection, and contactor interlocking.
fwdrev.op1: Press the Forward or Reverse push button to energize the selected direction circuit, provided the stop and safety contacts are closed.
fwdrev.op2: The star contactor connects the motor windings in star during the initial starting stage.
fwdrev.op3: After the timer delay, the star contactor releases and the circuit changes over to delta operation.
fwdrev.op4: The Stop button, Emergency Stop, or overload protection interrupts the control circuit and releases the contactors.
fwdrev.videoLabel: Project video · Electrical control and power schematic
fwdrev.videoNote: A visual walkthrough of the forward/reverse control circuit and star-delta power circuit.
fwdrev.safetyLead: Stop the motor and allow it to come to a complete stop before reversing direction.
fwdrev.safetyBody: Reversing while it is still spinning can create high electrical and mechanical stress, potentially damaging the motor and contactors.
fwdrev.improveBody: Add a suitable time-delay relay or dedicated reversing control system to prevent reverse operation until sufficient stopping time has elapsed. Select the delay for the motor and application. A timer alone does not confirm that the motor has actually stopped; the stopping time must be properly determined and verified.
fwdrev.engineering: This is an educational schematic, not a validated design for a real installation. All equipment ratings, protection, interlocking, and timing must be checked for the actual motor and application.
fwdrev.eng1: Choose protection and contactors based on the motor nameplate, circuit arrangement, prospective fault current, manufacturer guidance, and applicable standards.
fwdrev.eng2: Confirm the motor is suitable for star-delta starting at the available supply voltage.
fwdrev.eng3: Verify the electrical and mechanical interlocks, overload protection, earthing, and isolation before any real-world implementation.
fwdrev.learning: This project supports my continued development in industrial electrical control, instrumentation, and automation.

stardelta.eyebrow: Classic Electrical Control · Motor Starting · CADe SIMU
stardelta.title: Star-Delta Motor Starter
stardelta.cardDesc: A classic star-delta starter for a three-phase induction motor, with power and control circuits, timer-based changeover, self-holding and electrical interlocking.
stardelta.overview: This project presents a classic star-delta starter for a three-phase induction motor, designed and simulated in CADe SIMU. It includes the power circuit and the control circuit, illustrating contactor control, timer-based changeover, self-holding, and electrical interlocking.
stardelta.op1: Press START to energize the main contactor KM1 and timer relay T1, when the control conditions are satisfied.
stardelta.op2: The star contactor KM3 connects the motor windings in star during the initial starting period.
stardelta.op3: After the timer delay, the circuit releases the star contactor and changes over to delta operation through KM4.
stardelta.op4: STOP or an overload trip interrupts the control circuit and releases the contactors.
stardelta.videoNote: A short, silent visual demonstration of the power and control schematics.
stardelta.engineering: This is an educational schematic simulation, not a validated installation design. Every motor installation requires its own engineering checks.
stardelta.eng1: Select cable cross-section using motor current, installation method, cable length, ambient temperature, grouping, voltage drop, and short-circuit withstand.
stardelta.eng2: Select MCCB, MCB, contactors, and overload protection based on the motor nameplate, fault level, circuit arrangement, manufacturer guidance, and applicable standards.
stardelta.eng3: Confirm that the motor is suitable for star-delta starting at the available supply voltage, and provide suitable electrical and mechanical interlocking.
stardelta.eng4: Verify earthing, isolation, protection coordination, and the safety design before any real-world implementation.
stardelta.learning: This project supports my continued development in industrial electrical control, instrumentation, and automation.
